title: Why Your Data Dashboard Stinks
intro: Most teams stop at visual clarity: the chart renders, matches the design system and passes accessibility checks. Dashboards built that way still mislead, because human cognition is full of shortcuts.

learn.title: Five ways dashboards mislead
learn.text:
**1. Misleading continuity:** a line between two quarterly numbers looks like a trend.
**2. Accidental grouping:** things placed together look related.
**3. Colour assumptions:** red, green and yellow carry meaning whether intended or not.
**4. Memory overload:** comparisons hidden behind toggles and tabs.
**5. Anchoring and framing:** the first metric becomes the benchmark.

try.q: Two quarterly figures are joined by a line. What will users assume?
options: That something is trending between them
That the two figures are unrelated
That the data between them is incomplete or missing
That the second figure is the target
try.explain: Misleading continuity: people read a line as continuous change.

learn.title: Start from the decision
learn.text:
Ask **“What decisions do users need to make here?”** before “What data do we have?”

When a dashboard is built around decisions, structure becomes obvious: show only the data that supports the choice at hand.

Then map visuals to mental models. People expect bars to compare categories and lines to show change over time.

try.q: What should you ask first when designing a dashboard?
options: What decisions do users need to make here?
What data do we already have available?
Which chart types does the library support?
How many metrics fit above the fold?

learn.title: Compare side by side, and label
learn.text:
If users need to compare metrics, **place them next to each other**. Never hide them behind toggles or tabs: the moment someone has to remember a number, errors follow.

“Think of comparison as a visual task, not a cognitive one.”

And use labels, not just legends, so every chart explains itself.

try.q: Revenue is on one tab and cost on another. Users must compare them. What is the fix?
options: Show both metrics side by side
Add a tooltip with the other value
Use a brighter colour on each tab
Add a legend below the tab bar
try.explain: Comparison from memory is the “memory overload” problem.

test.q: A 98% success rate and a 2% failure rate feel different to users. Which effect is this?
options: Framing
Accidental grouping
Misleading continuity
Memory overload

test.q: Metric A drops and metric B, placed beside it, rises. What might users wrongly conclude?
options: That one caused the other
That both are measured weekly
That A is more important than B
That the dashboard has a bug
test.explain: Accidental grouping: proximity suggests a relationship.

test.q: Which chart do people expect for change over time?
options: A line chart
A bar chart
A pie chart
A table of totals
test.explain: Lines for change over time, bars for comparing categories.

test.q: Why is “the chart renders correctly and passes accessibility checks” not enough?
options: It ignores how users interpret and decide
Accessibility checks are usually wrong about charts
Rendering bugs always appear later
Design systems forbid most charts
test.explain: UX research adds how people interpret, compare and decide.

test.q: What does “use labels, not just legends” aim for?
options: Every chart is self-explanatory
Charts use fewer colours overall
Legends can be hidden on mobile
Users learn the colour code faster
test.explain: Direct labels remove the look-up step.
